 Judgment
This petition under Section 166 MV act is filed by the Petitioner seeking compensation of Rs.5,00,00,000/- for the injuries sustained by him in a road traffic accident.

2. It is the specific case of the petitioner that, on 20-02-2023, at about 8:00 p.m., he was riding his motorcycle bearing registration No.KA-34-EL-2817 along with a pillion rider on Bengaluru - Bellary main road, near Jakkuru cross signal, Yelahanka, Bengaluru.

At that time, the driver of a Innova Car bearing No.KA-03-AF-6668 (hereinafter referred to as the offending vehicle) drove the vehicle at a high speed in a rash and negligent manner, suddenly applied breaks and took his vehicle towards right side without giving any indication.
As a result, the petitioner, who was riding his motorcycle behind the car, attempted to control his vehicle but still came in contact with the rear portion of the car.
Due to the impact of the accident, the petitioner sustained grievous injuries and was immediately shifted to Prolife Multi speciality Hospital, Bengaluru, where he underwent inpatient treatment.
Thereafter, he was shifted to Mahaveer Jain hospital, Bengaluru, where he further underwent inpatient treatment and surgery.
3. The petitioner submits that, due to the injuries sustained in the accident, he has suffered permanent disability and is unable to lead a normal life as he did prior to the accident.
He claims to have incurred huge expenses towards medical treatment, medicines, conveyance, and incidental charges.

4. At the time of the accident, the petitioner was 23 years old, studying the course of PGDM at M.S.Ramaiah Institute of Management, Bengaluru and got offer as Engagement Financial Administrator at Deloitte USI Co., Bengaluru and his CTC was fixed Rs.7,60,000/- p.a.
He submits that, due to the accidental injuries, he has suffered permanent disability, lost his earning capacity and income.
5. The accident occurred solely due to the negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle.
Therefore, the petitioner prays that suitable compensation be awarded against Respondent No. 1 (owner) and Respondent No. 2 (insurer) of the offending vehicle.
6. In response to the petition notice, the Respondent No.2 has appeared through counsel and filed the written statement.
The Respondent No.1 did not turn up and was placed exparte.

7. The Respondent No.2 has filed its written statement by admitting the issuance of policy however,
its liability if any is subject to terms and conditions of the policy.
Respondent no 2 has contended that the owner of the alleged offending vehicle and the concerned police have not complied the mandatory provisions of Sec.134(c) and 158(6) of MV Act.
8. It has denied that the accident has occurred due to the negligence of driver of offending vehicle and other averments of the petition.

Respondent no. 2 further contended that the accident occurred solely due to the negligence of the petitioner himself, as he went and hit to the car from behind and tortfeasor cannot make benefit out of his own negligence and he had no valid DL at the time of accident.
Further, the concerned police filed a charge sheet against the petitioner, thereby establishing that the accident occurred due to his fault.
Hence, Respondent No.2 submits that it is not liable to pay any compensation to the petitioner.
It has contended that the driver of the offending vehicle had no valid DL.

It has disputed that the nature of injuries sustained by the Petitioner, the petitioner's avocation, income, future income, medical expenses claimed by him and the disability suffered by him and has therefore prayed for dismissal of the petition.

9. On the basis of the above pleadings, the following Issues were framed :-
1.

Whether the Petitioner proves that he sustained injuries when he was riding his motorcycle bearing No.KA-34-EL-2817 on 20-02-2023 about 8.00 p.m. near Jakkur Cross signal, BB Main road, Yelahanka, Bengaluru District, only due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of Innova Car bearing No.KA-03-AF-6668?
2. What compensation Petitioner is entitled?
3. What order ?
10. In order to prove the claim, the Petitioner examined as PW.1 and in support of his case, 6 witnesses are examined as PW-2 to 7 and got marked the documents as per Ex.P.1 to P.54 respectively.
11. Respondent No.2 has examined the IO as RW-1 and the official of respondent No.2 is examined as RW-2 and her authorization letter is marked as Ex.R.1.

12. By considering the available materials on record and the arguments addressed by the parties, I have answered the above Issues as under:
Issue No.1: Partly in the Affirmative.
Issue No.2: Partly in affirmative.

Issue No.3: As per the final order, for the following:
REASONS 13. ISSUE NO.1:-

The petitioner has specifically pleaded that on 22.02.2023 at about 8:00 p.m., he was riding his motorcycle bearing No. KA-34-EL-2817 along with a pillion rider on the Suhasa.V vs Sathya Moorthy.S on 3 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22472926/
3 Bengaluru-Bellary Road near Jakkuru Cross Signal, Bengaluru.

At that time, the driver of the offending car allegedly drove the vehicle at a high speed in a rash and negligent manner, suddenly applied brakes, and turned the vehicle towards the right side without giving any indicator or signal.
As a result, the petitioner, who was riding immediately behind the car, attempted to control his motorcycle but still came into contact with the rear portion of the car.
Due to the impact, the accident occurred and the petitioner sustained multiple injuries.

14. To substantiate his case, the petitioner examined as PW-1, who filed an affidavit under Order 18 Rule 4 CPC and produced police documents marked as Ex.P-1 to P-14. PW-2, the MRO from Pro- Life Multi-speciality Hospital, produced Ex.P-34 to P- 38; PW-3 from Sakra Hospital produced Ex.P-39 and P-40; PW-4, the MRD Assistant from Bhagawan Mahavir Jain Hospital, produced Ex.P-41 to P-47; and PW-7, Dr. Veeresh U. Mathad, produced Ex.P-50 to P- 54.
seriously contended that the petitioner himself was solely negligent, and that he struck the car from behind because he failed to maintain a safe distance.
It was further contended that the FIR was initially registered against the petitioner and that the allegations in the complaint also suggested negligence on the part of the petitioner.
Respondent No. 2 argued that the IO filed the charge-sheet against the car driver without proper investigation.
16. This being a civil claim under the Motor Vehicles Act, the standard of proof is preponderance of probabilities.
Therefore, the tribunal is required to appreciate the credible oral and documentary evidence to determine negligence.
17. In this context, examination of the FIR becomes important.
The FIR in the present case was neither lodged by the petitioner nor his family members, nor any independent witness, but by the driver of the offending car himself.
No prudent person would ordinarily lodge a complaint admitting his own negligence.
Therefore, the FIR, by its very nature, cannot be treated as conclusive evidence establishing rash or negligent driving on the part of the petitioner.
It only reflects a self-serving version narrated by the car driver at the earliest point in time.
Hence, the FIR cannot be relied upon to conclude that the car driver was not negligent.
18. To substantiate the contention, the Respondent No. 2 examined its official as RW2.
He reiterated the contention of the written statement and the IO as RW-1.
RW1 stated that he conducted a thorough investigation, recorded the statements of eyewitnesses, inspected the spot, drew the mahazar, and collected relevant material.
Based on the entire evidence gathered during the investigation, After appreciation of the totality of evidence, he filed a charge-sheet against both the car driver and the petitioner.
19. On perusal of charge-sheet it appears that the accident occurred due to the negligence of both the car driver and the petitioner.
Further it becomes clear that the car driver was predominantly responsible for the accident, as he suddenly applied brakes and turned the car to the right without giving any indication.
Had he not done so, the accident could have been avoided.

During the course of cross examination, the IO admitted certain omissions, such as failure to collect CCTV footage from the signal and not obtaining call records of Yoga Srinivas.
He also stated that the motorcycle hit the rear side of the car.
However, such omissions by itself cannot lead to the conclusion that the IO failed to conduct a proper investigation.
An FIR often contains only the initial version.
subsequent through examination of eyewitnesses, collection of material on record and drawing of spot mahazar, presents a more accurate and complete picture of the accident.

Therefore,
the finding emerging from a thorough investigation carry greater evidentiary value than the bare recitals in the FIR.
21. During cross-examination, suggestions were put to the petitioner that the accident occurred solely due to his negligence; however, the petitioner denied the same.
22. The respondent no 2 has not produced any independent, cogent evidence to show that the IO falsely implicated the car driver colluded with the petitioner.

If Respondent No. 2 wanted to prove that the petitioner was solely negligent, they were required to produce independent evidence such as eyewitnesses, CCTV footage and photographs showing petitioner's rash conduct.
No such convincing material has been placed on record.
Thus, absence of CCTV footage or call records does not automatically weaken the petitioner's case.
It only means that the investigation lacked certain elements, but this alone is not enough to discredit the final charge-sheet.
23. The IMV report clearly establishes that there was no mechanical defect in the car involved in the accident.

It is evident from the material on record that the car driver suddenly applied brakes and turned towards the right side without giving any signal, and at the same time, the rider of the motorcycle was travelling at a high speed and without maintaining a safe distance, due to which he dashed against the rear right portion of the car.
24. By producing police documents, the petitioner attempted to impress upon the Tribunal that the accident occurred solely due to the negligent driving of the car driver.

On the other hand,
respondent No. 2, in his written statement as well as RW2 in his evidence, attempted to show that the accident was caused solely due to the negligence of the petitioner.

Respondent No. 2 has relied upon the decision reported in 2007 AIR SCW 3591, Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. v. Premalatha Shukla and Others, wherein it is held that once a document is brought on record and any part of its contents is admitted in evidence, the party producing the same cannot subsequently contend that the remaining contents have not been proved.
25.

Another decision relied upon is the judgment reported in 2014 AIR SCW 1081, Lachoo Ram &
Others v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation, wherein the Supreme Court held that allegations of rash and negligent driving cannot be accepted when the evidence on record shows that the deceased motorcyclist, while attempting to overtake the bus, had gone to its right side and was not visible to the driver.

5 26.

On the other hand, the petitioner has relied upon the decision in SLP No. 28062-63 of 2023,
S.Mohammed Hakkim v. National Insurance Company Ltd., wherein the Supreme Court held that if a car driver suddenly stops his vehicle in the middle of a national highway, such conduct cannot be treated as reasonable.

entities.text: S.Mohammed Hakkim v. National Insurance Company Ltd.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Vehicles on highways are expected to move at high speed, and therefore the driver intending to stop must give proper warning or signal.
In that case, since no precautions were taken by the car driver, he was held negligent.
27. In the case of Lachoo, the respondent had examined eye-witnesses who categorically stated that the accident did not occur due to the negligence of the bus driver.
In the present case, the respondent no 2 has examined any the eye-witnesses to substantiate its contention.
Materials clearly establish that the accident occurred because the driver of the car applied sudden brakes, took a right turn without any indication, and failed to give proper signal.
Respondent No. 2 has failed to disprove this fact, whereas the petitioner has successfully established that the car driver was primarily responsible for the accident 28.
Furthermore, in Mohammed Hakkim, the Supreme Court's observations were in the context of vehicles moving on a national highway, where high speed is expected.

In the present case, however,
the accident occurred within city limits where high speed is not expected.
If the motorcyclist was riding at a moderate speed, he could have controlled his vehicle.
Therefore, there was contributory negligence on his part as well.
Hence, the decisions of Lachoo and Mohammaed Hakkim do not squarely apply to the facts of the present case.
29. Based on the entire material gathered during investigation, it became clear that the car driver was primarily responsible for the accident.
Had the car driver not suddenly applied brakes and turned towards the right without giving any signal, the accident could have been avoided.
After appreciating the entirety of the evidence, the investigating officer filed a charge sheet holding both the car driver and the petitioner responsible.
30. Considering all the evidence, this Tribunal finds that the dominant cause of the accident was the rash and negligent driving of the car driver.
The material on record support this conclusion.
At the same time, the record also shows that the petitioner was riding the motorcycle at a high speed.
Had he exercised proper caution and maintained a safe distance, he could have avoided the impact.
Therefore, the petitioner also contributed to the occurrence of the accident.

31. In view of the manner in which the accident occurred, and considering that the offending vehicle is a car while the petitioner was riding the motorcycle at high speed, this Tribunal finds it just and proper to fasten 25% contributory negligence on the petitioner and 75% negligence on the car driver.
32 . As rightly contended by respondent No. 2, the petitioner cannot accept only the favourable parts of the police documents and ignore the portions which are against him.
The principles of evidence do not permit selective reliance.
Therefore, considering all aspects, the plea of the petitioner that the accident occurred solely due to the negligence of the car driver cannot be accepted.

Thus, on a careful appreciation of the evidence, the Tribunal holds that this is a case of contributory negligence.

Considering the manner of the accident, the conduct of both parties, and the degree of causal contribution, the Tribunal apportions negligence as follows: Driver of the offending car :
75% (primary negligence, Petitioner/rider of the motorcycle: 25% (contributory negligence).
Accordingly Issue No.1 is answered in the partly Affirmative.

34. ISSUE NO.2 :- As per the medical records, the petitioner sustained mild head injury, D5-D6 vertebral body fracture-dislocation, injuries to both lower limbs resulting in paraplegia, left medial one- third clavicle fracture with SDH, and right pleural effusion.

There was also a fracture of the L3 vertebral body, with complete disruption of the spinal column due to fracture involving the posterior aspect of D6 vertebral body, resulting in spinal cord transection.
The treating doctors opined that all these injuries are grievous in nature.

35. Immediately after the accident, the petitioner was admitted to Profile Multi-Specialty Hospital,
Bengaluru, where he was treated as an inpatient.
He was subsequently shifted to Mahaveer Jain Hospital for further management, where he underwent two major surgeries.

Post-surgery, he received physiotherapy and occupational therapy at Sakra World Hospital, and was later advised follow-up treatment with Ayurvedic medicines at DGM Ayurvedic Medical College Hospital, Gadag.

sentences.text: Subsequently, he was admitted at the Association of People with Disabilities, Horticulture Training Center, Jeevan Bhima Nagar, Bengaluru, where he was trained in performing activities of daily living with minimal dependence.

36. The petitioner was examined by Dr. Veeresh U. Mathad, Senior Consultant Neurosurgeon,
Manipal Hospital (PW-7), who produced clinical notes, MRI reports, X-ray films, and related documentation (Exhibits P-50 to P-54).

PW-7 deposed that the petitioner met with a road traffic accident on 22.02.2023, resulting in injuries to the head, spine, chest, and left shoulder, along with loss of sensation and power in both lower limbs and transient loss of consciousness.

At the time of admission at Bhagwan Mahaveer Jain Hospital, the petitioner was conscious, obeying commands,
with a GCS score of E4V5M6, but had 0/5 power in both lower limbs, no sensation below the nipple level, and involvement of bowel and bladder.
Tenderness over the dorsal spine was noted.

37. PW-7 further stated that the petitioner sustained polytrauma, including severe traumatic brain injury, D5-D6 vertebral fracture-dislocation, spinal cord transection, right pleural effusion with pneumothorax, left clavicle fracture, mild acute SDH, and cerebral oedema.

Surgical interventions included D2-D8 bilateral pedicle screw instrumentation, decompression, bilateral facetectomy,
laminectomy, neurolysis and adhesiolysis of dura and nerve roots, and reduction of fracture, along with ORIF of the left clavicle and right ICD insertion for pneumothorax.

Post-surgery, he remained in ICU on ventilator support and was provided with ongoing physiotherapy, neuro- rehabilitation,
and wheelchair mobilization.
At discharge, the petitioner remained conscious but paraplegic, with complete loss of power in both lower limbs and continued catheterization.

7 38.

The petitioner subsequently underwent long- term rehabilitation at Sakra World Hospital (06.03.2023 to 04.05.2023), DGM Ayurvedic Medical College Hospital, Gadag (15.05.2023 to 26.09.2023), and the Association of People with Disabilities for three months.

entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: PW-7 examined the petitioner for Neurological Disability Assessment on 21.12.2024.
He confirmed that prior to the accident, the petitioner was apparently healthy, fully mobile, and able to perform daily and vocational activities.

Post-accident, the petitioner has complete loss of power below the chest, trunk weakness, inability to get up or walk, loss of voluntary control over urination and defecation, and requires continuous attendant support.
He is wheelchair-bound and unable to perform his occupation as a priest.

39. Clinical examination establish that the petitioner has completely lost sensation below the D5 spinal segment, has no control over bowel and bladder functions, and has sustained a complete transection of the spinal cord, resulting in permanent and irreversible neurological disability.

PW-7 has opined that the petitioner suffers from 100% functional disability, rendering him entirely dependent on others for survival and all basic daily activities, and incapable of performing any form of independent work.

40. Although PW-7 did not treat the petitioner from the date of accident and did not obtain a separate orthopedic opinion, his disability assessment is based on a thorough review of the operative notes, medical records, radiological films, and clinical evaluation conducted at the time of examination.

The cumulative evidence clearly establishes that the petitioner's disability is critical,
permanent, and total, leading to a complete loss of earning capacity.

41. Considering that the injuries involve the D5 and D6 levels of the upper thoracic spine segments crucial for spinal stability, movement, trunk control, and neurological functioning- the resulting impairment is severe and life-long.
The petitioner has suffered total loss of power in both lower limbs, inability to perform daily activities, and complete dependency on others for even the most basic functions.
It is evident that he can no longer engage in any form of gainful employment or independent livelihood.

42. The Tribunal observes that, in cases of spinal cord injury, functional disability must be assessed on the basis of actual loss of functional capacity, vocational incapacity, requirement of continuous assistance, and permanence of impairment, rather than merely on numerical percentages.

In the present case, the petitioner is unable to move independently, requires continuous nursing care,
cannot resume his previous vocation, and remains wheelchair-bound with total loss of motor power in both lower limbs.
His clinical condition is consistent with complete and permanent functional disability.

43. Accordingly, the Tribunal holds that the petitioner has suffered 100% functional disability,
which is permanent, severe, and requiring ongoing medical care, nursing support, and attendant assistance for all daily living activities.
Functional disability of the petitioner is therefore assessed at 100% for both occupational and daily living purposes.

45. On perusal of Exhibit P-23, it appears that the petitioner was shortlisted and selected for the said post and was requested to report for joining.

The petitioner further contends that due to the injuries suffered in the accident, he was compelled to decline the offer, and although the company provided several opportunities to re-join, he could not resume the employment because of his disability.

He has produced Ex.P.32 - E-mail correspondence between the Institution and Deloitte Support Services Pvt. Ltd., which also indicates that the petitioner was given multiple opportunities to join service.

46. However, the learned counsel for the respondents argued that the petitioner has not produced any formal appointment letter, and therefore, the placement letter and email communications should not be considered.
During cross-examination, PW-1 admitted that he had only received a resume/selection letter and that he had not actually joined the job.
The respondents therefore contend that the petitioner's claim of a fixed annual salary of 7,60,000 cannot be accepted.
47. In contrast, the petitioner has argued that if the accident had not occurred, he would have undoubtedly joined the organization, obtained the appointment letter, and commenced his employment.

The petitioner was pursuing the PGDM at M.S.Ramaiah Institute of Management,
Bengaluru selected for a prestigious position, the court ought to consider his realistic earning potential rather than rejecting the claim for want of an appointment letter.

48. To support his contention, the petitioner relied on the decision in Civil Special Appeal No.
18337/2021, Muralidhar v. Subbalakshmi & Another, wherein the Hon'ble Court held that even in the absence of a formal proof of salary, when a claimant is a qualified individual with demonstrated employability, the tribunal can reasonably determine notional income based on educational qualifications, employment prospects, and contemporaneous circumstances.

In that case, although the accident occurred in 2013 and there was no strict proof of salary, the Court held that a student with comparable qualifications would earn at least 20,000 per month and therefore adopted that figure as notional income in the interest of justice, applying the principles laid down in Sarala Verma v. DTC and National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi.

49. Keeping in view of submission of the petitioner, this Tribunal observes the following:
1. The PGDM petitioner is a PGDM graduate.
2. He was selected after a competitive campus recruitment process.
3. Exhibit P-33, emails produced corroborate that the offer was genuine.

4. The accident occurred immediately before his expected date of joining.
5. There is no material from the respondents to show that the petitioner would not have been issued a formal appointment letter.

50. Therefore, although the petitioner has not produced an actual appointment letter, the fact that he was selected for a job with a CTC of 7,60,000 per annum reflects his employability and future earning prospects.
Resuming employment was prevented solely due to the disability caused by the accident.

51. Considering his educational background, the nature of the job offered, the documentary evidence, and the principles governing notional income, this Tribunal deems it reasonable and just to fix his income at 40,000 per month for the purpose of computing loss of future income.
52. The Petitioner has stated that he was aged about 23 years, in support of his age he has produced his Aadhar card at Ex.P.22, which shows his date of birth as 15-01-2001 .
Therefore, as on date of accident his age is considered as 22 years.

Therefore, the proper multiplier applicable to the case on hand is 18.
53.

In the case MFA No 103807/2016 C/w MFA 103835/2016 New India Assurance Company Ltd V Abdul and another Hon'ble High court has held that once permanent disability affecting earning capacity is established, the victim is entitled to be compensated not only for the present loss of income but also for the future loss of earnings and prospects, taking into account his age, avocation,
and the multiplier applicable.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 54. In case of Pappu Deo Yadav v Naresh Kumar and others 2020 SCC online SC 752 the Apex court held that in the case of permanent partial disability amount towards future prospects can be awarded .

entities.text: Pappu Deo Yadav v Naresh Kumar and others 2020 SCC online SC 752
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The said preposition of law has been reiterated by the Hon'ble High court reported in 2020 SCC online KAR 1446 between Alameli Bai V/s Managing Director KSRTC, wherein the Hon'ble High court of Karnataka has held that in case of functional disability cases, future prospects can be awarded.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus the petitioner is entitled for the amount towards future prospects.
55. Keeping in view above said principles this tribunal concludes that the petitioner was 22 years as on the date of the alleged accident.
As such, 40% of the future prospects is to be added to the annual income.
Thus effective notional income comes to Rs.40,000 + 40% = 56,000/- per month.

56. Further the petitioner was aged about 22 years as on date of alleged accident and the multiplier applicable to the petitioner as per decision laid down by Hon'ble Apex court in Sarla Verma's case is at 18.
The loss of future earnings comes to Rs 56,000 x 12 x 18 x 100/100= .1,20,96,000/-.
57. Pain and sufferings:
The learned counsel for the petitioner has contended that the petitioner sustained grievous spinal cord injury resulting in severe neurological deficit.
It is submitted that the Suhasa.V vs Sathya Moorthy.

S on 3 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/22472926/
10 term "pain and suffering" encompasses not only physical discomfort and distress but also the mental and emotional trauma suffered as a consequence of the injuries.

The learned counsel has further argued that pain and suffering is a recognized head of compensation under motor accident claims, and while it cannot be measured in terms of money through any precise mathematical calculation, courts are empowered to award just compensation under this head by way of conventional sums.
58.
In the present case, the medical evidence clearly establishes that the petitioner is completely bedridden, he lost his power and remains wholly dependent upon a catheter for urination .
He requires constant nursing care and assistance even for the most basic activities of daily life.
His life has thus been reduced to a state of total dependency without mobility.

59. Therefore, taking into account the petitioner's complete loss of independence, lifelong suffering,
this Tribunal considers that a sum of 5,00,000/- would be just, fair, and reasonable compensation under the head of pain and suffering.
60. Loss of amenities of life: undoubtedly the petitioner is suffering from difficulties in performing day to day activities and is facing continuous hardship due to the disability.
Therefore this tribunal finds to appropriate to award a sum .1,00,000/- under head of loss of amenities of life.
61. Medical expenses:

Under the head of pecuniary damages relating to treatment, hospitalization,
and purchase of medicines, the petitioner has relied upon Exhibit P-25, amounting to Rs. 15,87,814,
and Exhibit P-13, amounting to Rs. 3,50,345.
Though learned counsel for Respondent No. 2 cross-examined PW-1 at length, nothing substantial was elicited to discredit or dispute the genuineness of the medical bills produced by the petitioner.
Upon careful scrutiny of Exhibit P-13, it is noted that an amount of Rs. 2,62,000 pertains to attender/attendance charges.
Since attender charges are separately considered under a distinct head, the said amount is excluded from medical expenses and will be dealt with appropriately under the head of attendant charges.

Apart from this exclusion, all remaining medical bills appear to be genuine, consistent with the nature of injuries sustained, duration of hospitalization, surgeries undergone, and subsequent rehabilitation.

Accordingly, the petitioner is entitled to be reimbursed towards medical expenses a sum of Rs.
16,76,185/-

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Therefore, the tribunal is required to appreciate the credible oral and documentary evidence to determine negligence.
17. In this context, examination of the FIR becomes important.
The FIR in the present case was neither lodged by the petitioner nor his family members, nor any independent witness, but by the driver of the offending car himself.
No prudent person would ordinarily lodge a complaint admitting his own negligence.
Therefore, the FIR, by its very nature, cannot be treated as conclusive evidence establishing rash or negligent driving on the part of the petitioner.
It only reflects a self-serving version narrated by the car driver at the earliest point in time.
Hence, the FIR cannot be relied upon to conclude that the car driver was not negligent.
An FIR often contains only the initial version.
subsequent through examination of eyewitnesses, collection of material on record and drawing of spot mahazar, presents a more accurate and complete picture of the accident.
Therefore,
the finding emerging from a thorough investigation carry greater evidentiary value than the bare recitals in the FIR.
21. During cross-examination, suggestions were put to the petitioner that the accident occurred solely due to his negligence; however, the petitioner denied the same.
If Respondent No. 2 wanted to prove that the petitioner was solely negligent, they were required to produce independent evidence such as eyewitnesses, CCTV footage and photographs showing petitioner's rash conduct.
No such convincing material has been placed on record.
Thus, absence of CCTV footage or call records does not automatically weaken the petitioner's case.
It only means that the investigation lacked certain elements, but this alone is not enough to discredit the final charge-sheet.
Another decision relied upon is the judgment reported in 2014 AIR SCW 1081, Lachoo Ram &
Others v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation, wherein the Supreme Court held that allegations of rash and negligent driving cannot be accepted when the evidence on record shows that the deceased motorcyclist, while attempting to overtake the bus, had gone to its right side and was not visible to the driver.
